newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS- Palladium, copper hit highs in commodities.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS- Palladium, copper hit highs in commodities.

text.p: The world price of palladium hit its highest since the start of the 1990s on Tuesday and copper raced up to its strongest for a year, both helped up by revived speculative fund interest.

Palladium, a rare white metal used mainly in electronics and for making catalytic converters, rose to $179.75 an ounce, the highest since 1989, on shortages from Russia and fund buying, after opening the day at $174.
"It's to do with (Russian) non-delivery, Tokyo (futures market) positions and fund interest all happening together," one dealer said.
The market is concerned about dwindling stockpiles of palladium in Russia, the leading producer. There have also been administrative delays to Russian exports to Japan, the biggest user.
A quiet end to rangebound trading on the London Metal Exchange was interrupted by a late burst in copper which steamed to a one-year high in a matter of minutes.
Three-months copper hit a high of $2,507 per tonne on short-covering and fund buying, against a previous close of $2,463.

A buoyant U.S. economy is good for metals demand, and analysts said the market may have been assuming that the Federal Reserve Board Open Market Committee was going to leave interest rates unchanged on Tuesday.
The price of coffee futures, on which a blistering rally made headlines over the last week, eased.
Prices for the London-traded robusta bean type, used in instant blends, fell to a day's low of $2,045 a tonne, down $55 from Monday, on the July contract. It recovered a bit later to end $25 down.
New York futures for higher quality arabica beans also fell, with July dropping as far as $2.39 per pound from the open of $2.43 before recovering to hover a couple of cents down.
Producer nations, meeting in London, mulled the potentially disastrous downturn that a change in tide of fund interest would cause world coffee prices that have risen by 80-100 percent since January.
Low stocks, tight supply from Colombia and fears that Brazil, the biggest exporter, may have another frost hooked speculators and triggered coffee's longest sustained rally for two decades.
The rally was propelled by fund buying but it would be unlikely they would sell ahead of the Brazilian winter (August) which could have a drastic effect on supply from the number one producer.
The price of gold fixed at $343.00 an ounce compared to the open of $342.75 and Monday's $340 low.
Analysts said it would struggle to get above $350.
Benchmark IPE North Sea Brent crude fell in the morning to a low of $19.84 per barrel but pulled back up above $20.20 later.
The jump was triggered by reports that Turkish Kurdish rebels had attacked a small oil installation in southeast Turkey.
Wheat futures on the Chicago Board of Trade were down a couple of cents a bushel, on the prospect of rain in the growing areas of western Kansas.
